title: Giant Cell Arteritis, Takayasu, Polyarteritis Nodosa, Kawasaki, and GPA

steps.tx: Giant cell arteritis, historically termed temporal arteritis, is the most frequent systemic vasculitis in older adults, occurring almost exclusively in patients older than fifty years of age with a two-to-one female predilection. The granulomatous inflammation selectively targets large and medium-sized arteries, displaying a marked predilection for branches of the carotid artery: the superficial temporal, ophthalmic, and vertebral arteries, alongside the thoracic aorta. Patients present with new-onset unremitting unilateral headache, scalp tenderness when brushing hair, jaw claudication upon mastication, and **striking erythrocyte sedimentation rate elevation** typically exceeding eighty millimeters per hour.
steps.say: Giant cell arteritis is the most common vasculitis in patients over age fifty, with women affected twice as often as men. It targets large and medium cranial branches of the carotid artery, especially the superficial temporal and ophthalmic arteries. Patients present with severe unilateral headache, jaw fatigue while chewing called jaw claudication, and exquisite scalp tenderness when brushing their hair. Blood tests characteristically reveal an erythrocyte sedimentation rate exceeding eighty to one hundred millimeters per hour.

vis.caption: Giant cell arteritis histopathology with giant cells at the internal elastic lamina.

steps.tx: The definitive diagnostic reference standard is an **excisional temporal artery biopsy**, requiring a surgical segment of at least two to three centimeters because inflammation is segmental and patchy (skip lesions). Histopathological examination reveals granulomatous panarteritis centered upon the internal elastic lamina. Dense infiltrates of CD4-positive T-lymphocytes and macrophages are accompanied by multinucleated foreign-body or Langhans giant cells in seventy-five percent of biopsies. The internal elastic lamina undergoes marked fragmentation and elastolysis, while reactive intimal fibroplasia severely narrows the vascular lumen, predisposing to ischemic optic neuropathy.
steps.say: The gold standard for diagnosing giant cell arteritis is a superficial temporal artery biopsy. Because the vasculitis is patchy and discontinuous, forming skip lesions, the surgeon must remove a generous two-to-three-centimeter segment. Under the microscope, granulomatous inflammation attacks the internal elastic lamina, featuring CD4 T-cells, macrophages, and multinucleated giant cells. The internal elastic lamina is chewed away and fragmented, while intimal proliferation chokes off the vascular lumen.

left.title: Giant Cell Arteritis Histology
points: Granulomatous panarteritis centered on internal elastic lamina
Multinucleated foreign-body and Langhans giant cells (75%)
Prominent fragmentation and elastolysis of elastic fibers
Marked intimal hyperplasia causing luminal stenosis

right.title: Skip Lesion Diagnostic Trap
points: Inflammation is segmental and discontinuous along artery
Normal histology can alternate with dense granulomas
Biopsy must sample 2 to 3 cm of temporal artery
Serial sectioning by pathologist mandatory to prevent false-negatives

steps.tx: Takayasu arteritis, historically termed **pulseless disease of Takayasu**, is a chronic granulomatous panarteritis of large elastic arteries striking females younger than forty years, predominantly of Asian descent. Inflammation targets the aortic arch and its primary brachiocephalic branches, alongside the pulmonary and renal arteries. Transmural granulomatous inflammation and adventitial fibrosis cause marked concentric fibrous thickening that severely stenoses arch branch ostia. Patients manifest markedly diminished or absent radial and brachial pulses, disparate blood pressures between arms exceeding ten millimeters of mercury, upper limb claudication, and visual disturbances.
steps.say: Takayasu arteritis, or pulseless disease, is a granulomatous vasculitis of the aorta and its major branches that strikes young females under age forty. Heavy fibrous scarring and inflammation choke the origins of the carotid and subclavian arteries. Patients present with absent or weak radial pulses, unequal blood pressure measurements between the arms, and arm claudication during activity. Narrowing of the renal arteries causes severe secondary hypertension, while carotid stenosis produces syncope and visual changes.

vis.alt: Aortogram and anatomical diagram showing coarctation and branch vessel stenosis in Takayasu arteritis
vis.caption: Takayasu arteritis vascular lesions across aorta and primary branches.

steps.tx: Polyarteritis nodosa is a systemic necrotizing vasculitis targeting small and medium-sized muscular arteries, characteristically involving renal, coronary, and mesenteric circulations while **sparing pulmonary arterial beds**. Thirty percent of patients harbor chronic active hepatitis B virus infection with circulating hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg)-antibody immune complexes that deposit in arterial bifurcations. Patients present with acute systemic symptoms: refractory hypertension from renal artery involvement, abdominal angina and bloody diarrhoea from bowel ischemia, diffuse myalgias, and peripheral mononeuritis multiplex affecting peroneal and radial nerves.
steps.say: Polyarteritis nodosa is a necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized muscular arteries that attacks visceral organs like the kidneys, heart, and intestines. A vital negative invariant is that it completely spares the pulmonary circulation. Roughly thirty percent of cases are triggered by hepatitis B immune complexes. Renal artery microaneurysms cause severe renin-dependent hypertension, mesenteric ischemia causes abdominal angina, and peripheral nerve ischemia produces foot drop or wrist drop, termed mononeuritis multiplex.

rows: Ischemic necrosis of vasa nervorum in nerve trunks
Nerve conduction studies, sural nerve biopsy
Clean chest radiograph excludes GPA and MPA

steps.tx: The pathognomonic histological hallmark of polyarteritis nodosa is the coexistence of **different evolutionary stages of vascular lesions** within the same vessel or across different arteries simultaneously. Acute lesions demonstrate transmural necrotizing inflammation with bright pink fibrinoid necrosis and mixed neutrophil-macrophage infiltrates, destroying the internal elastic lamina. Concurrently, older lesions display fibrovascular healing, intimal proliferation, and dense fibrous adventitial scarring. Weakening of the necrotic muscularis media produces localized aneurysmal outpouchings alternating with stenotic fibrous segments, creating a classic rosary-bead appearance on mesenteric angiography.
steps.say: What makes polyarteritis nodosa histologically unique is that acute and chronic lesions coexist side by side. In one vessel segment, you see acute transmural fibrinoid necrosis and neutrophils. In an adjacent segment, the inflammation has already healed into dense fibrous scar tissue. The acutely weakened wall balloons outward into tiny aneurysms, alternating with fibrous narrowed zones. On visceral angiography, this alternation looks like a string of beads, often called the rosary-bead sign.

steps.tx: Kawasaki disease, formerly termed mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, is an acute, self-limited febrile vasculitis of infancy and early childhood, with eighty percent of cases occurring in children younger than five years of age. Diagnosis requires prolonged, remittent fever lasting at least five consecutive days plus four of five **diagnostic clinical criteria**: bilateral non-exudative bulbar conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes (strawberry tongue, erythematous cracked lips), polymorphous non-vesicular trunk exanthem, acute non-purulent cervical lymphadenopathy (>1.5 cm), and peripheral extremity changes (erythema and edema followed by periungual desquamation).
steps.say: Kawasaki disease is an acute febrile vasculitis of infants and toddlers under age five. The diagnosis is clinical, requiring high fever lasting at least five days plus four out of five key physical signs: red eyes without pus, a bright red strawberry tongue with cracked lips, a blotchy trunk rash, swollen lymph nodes in the neck, and swollen hands and feet with peeling skin around the fingernails. Recognizing it early is vital because untreated children develop life-threatening coronary artery aneurysms.

left.title: Kawasaki Diagnostic Criteria
points: Strawberry tongue, erythema of pharynx, cracked red lips
Edema and erythema of hands/feet with periungual peeling

right.title: Supporting Clinical Laboratory Signs
points: Elevated ESR, CRP, and serum ferritin levels

steps.tx: The paramount clinical danger in Kawasaki disease is acute vasculitis targeting coronary arteries. Up to twenty-five percent of untreated children develop **coronary artery aneurysms**, resulting from transmural infiltration of neutrophils and CD8-positive lymphocytes destroying medial elastic tissue. Aneurysms predispose to acute luminal thrombosis and fatal myocardial infarction. Early administration of high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g/kg) combined with aspirin within ten days reduces coronary aneurysm risk down to under four percent.
steps.say: The most dangerous complication of Kawasaki disease is coronary artery vasculitis. Without treatment, a quarter of affected children develop coronary artery aneurysms that can thrombose and cause fatal heart attacks in toddlers. Administering high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin alongside aspirin within the first ten days of fever halts coronary inflammation, dropping the aneurysm rate from twenty-five percent to under four percent, saving lives.

rows: 2 g/kg single intravenous infusion over 12 hr
Anti-inflammatory dose during acute febrile phase
Controls fever and suppresses acute vasculitis
Maintained until 6-8 weeks or indefinitely if aneurysms
Serial measurements of coronary artery internal diameter
Identifies ectasia and giant aneurysms (>8 mm)

steps.tx: Systemic vasculitides are standardized according to the **Chapel Hill Consensus Conference classification**, which categorizes vasculitis primarily by the predominant caliber of vessels involved. Large-vessel vasculitis encompasses giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis, targeting the aorta and its primary branches. Medium-vessel vasculitis comprises polyarteritis nodosa and Kawasaki disease, targeting main visceral muscular arteries. Small-vessel vasculitis is subdivided into ANCA-associated vasculitides (GPA, MPA, EGPA) characterized by pauci-immune necrotizing inflammation, and immune-complex-mediated vasculitides (IgA vasculitis, cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, and anti-GBM disease).
steps.say: The Chapel Hill Consensus Conference classifies vasculitis based on vessel size. Large-vessel vasculitides include giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis, attacking the aorta and main cranial branches. Medium-vessel vasculitides include polyarteritis nodosa and Kawasaki disease, which attack muscular visceral arteries. Small-vessel vasculitides attack capillaries and arterioles, divided into pauci-immune ANCA-associated diseases like GPA and MPA, and immune-complex diseases like Henoch-Schonlein purpura.

quiz.q: What is the primary histological feature observed on temporal artery biopsy in giant cell arteritis?
options: Granulomatous panarteritis with multinucleated giant cells and internal elastic lamina fragmentation
Concentric laminated onion-skin smooth muscle proliferation with duplicated basement membranes
Segmental transmural fibrinoid necrosis with coexistence of acute and healed lesions
Obliterative endarteritis with dense perivascular plasma cell cuffs around vasa vasorum
quiz.explain: Giant cell arteritis is a granulomatous panarteritis targeting the internal elastic lamina, featuring macrophages, T-cells, and multinucleated giant cells causing elastolysis.

quiz.q: What serious coronary artery complication occurs in up to 25% of untreated children with Kawasaki disease?
options: Coronary artery ectasia and giant aneurysms predisposing to thrombosis and rupture
Severe calcific aortic stenosis with commissural fusion
Diffuse amyloid light-chain deposition within the subendocardium
Aschoff body myocarditis leading to complete atrioventricular heart block
quiz.explain: Kawasaki disease targets medium muscular arteries; untreated children face a 25% risk of developing coronary artery aneurysms that can thrombose or rupture.

quiz.q: Which major vascular bed is characteristically spared from vasculitic involvement in polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)?
quiz.explain: Polyarteritis nodosa characteristically attacks renal, mesenteric, and coronary arteries while strictly sparing the pulmonary arterial circulation.
